title: 1 Chronicles 13:1–14
context: 1 Chronicles 13:1–14 tells of David’s first attempt to bring the ark to Jerusalem. The parallel account is 2 Samuel 6:1–11. Chronicles adds an opening in which David consults the leaders and the assembly, invites the priests and Levites, and gives the reason “for we didn’t seek it in the days of Saul” (13:1–4). The two accounts differ in wording at several points, and these differences are named here rather than harmonized: Chronicles has Baalah, identified as Kiriath Jearim, where Samuel has Baale Judah (2 Samuel 6:2); Chidon’s threshing floor (13:9) where Samuel has Nacon (2 Samuel 6:6); and the reason “because he put his hand on the ark” (13:10) where Samuel has “for his error” (2 Samuel 6:7). Chronicles also places this first attempt before Hiram’s embassy and the Philistine wars (chapter 14), which 2 Samuel 5:11–25 narrates before the ark story; interpreters discuss whether Chronicles arranges the material by theme, and this draft does not decide. The law required the Levites to carry the holy things on their shoulders and forbade even the Kohathites to touch them (Numbers 4:15; 7:9), and David himself later names the failure (15:13). Both traditions read Uzza’s death soberly as a lesson about the holiness of God and the need to approach him on his terms, not as the act of an arbitrary deity, and this is shared ground between them.

verses.text: David consulted with the captains of thousands and of hundreds, even with every leader.
verses.arminianNotes:
David consults with the captains of thousands and of hundreds, even with every leader, before he acts. Chronicles opens the ark story with this consultation, which 2 Samuel 6 does not record.

Arminian readers note that David seeks the counsel and consent of Israel’s leaders, so that bringing up the ark becomes a shared and willing undertaking of the people rather than a decree simply imposed by the king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the king’s desire to restore the ark reflects a heart set on God’s presence at the center of national life, and that Chronicles portrays David as a leader who gathers the whole people around worship.

Both traditions read the consultation as wise and godly leadership and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: David said to all the assembly of Israel, “If it seems good to you, and if it is of the LORD our God, let’s send word everywhere to our brothers who are left in all the land of Israel, with whom the priests and Levites are in their cities that have pasture lands, that they may gather themselves to us.
verses.arminianNotes:
David proposes to the assembly that word be sent to their brothers throughout the land, including the priests and Levites in their cities, so that all may gather. He frames the plan with a double condition: “If it seems good to you, and if it is of the LORD our God”.

Arminian readers note that David treats the assembly as responsible partners whose agreement genuinely matters, while still placing their consent under the higher test of the LORD’s will.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David places the whole plan beneath the will of the LORD, and that the explicit mention of priests and Levites already points toward the proper ordering of worship that chapter 15 will make clear.

Both traditions see the verse as a model of seeking God’s will together with the counsel of his people, and neither divides over it.

verses.text: Also, let’s bring the ark of our God back to us again, for we didn’t seek it in the days of Saul.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David calls the assembly to bring the ark of God back, saying “we didn’t seek it in the days of Saul.” The ark had remained at Kiriath Jearim for a long time (1 Samuel 7:1–2).

Arminian readers note the honest admission of past neglect, and they see in the call a summons to renewed seeking that the people can and should answer, a theme that recurs throughout Chronicles.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the neglect of the ark fits Chronicles’ portrait of Saul as a king who “didn’t inquire of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 10:14), and that renewal begins when God stirs a desire for his presence in his chosen king.

Both traditions agree that seeking God lies at the heart of Chronicles’ message and read the verse as a call to wholehearted worship.

verses.text: All the assembly said that they would do so, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the assembly agrees to do it, “for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people.” The proposal wins unanimous support.

Arminian readers see a genuine and willing response of the whole community, and they note that the story will show how even a sincere and united plan still needs to be carried out according to what God has commanded.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the phrase stresses human approval, and that the following verses show that consensus, however sincere, is not the measure of right worship; God’s own ordinance governs how his presence is approached (compare 15:13).

Both traditions read the agreement as good in itself and as the setting for a hard lesson about holiness.

verses.text: So David assembled all Israel together, from the Shihor River of Egypt even to the entrance of Hamath, to bring God’s ark from Kiriath Jearim.
verses.arminianNotes:
David assembles all Israel, from the Shihor River of Egypt to the entrance of Hamath, to bring God’s ark from Kiriath Jearim. The exact identification of the Shihor and of the entrance of Hamath is debated, but the phrase marks the widest bounds of the land.

Arminian readers see a national gathering in which every part of the people is invited to share in honoring the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Chronicles emphasizes all Israel, while the parallel in 2 Samuel 6:1 speaks of thirty thousand chosen men, and they let each account keep its own emphasis rather than merging the two descriptions.

Both traditions read the verse as showing the importance of the ark for the whole covenant people and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: David went up with all Israel to Baalah, that is, to Kiriath Jearim, which belonged to Judah, to bring up from there God the LORD’s ark that sits above the cherubim, that is called by the Name.
verses.arminianNotes:
David goes up with all Israel to Baalah, that is, Kiriath Jearim, which belonged to Judah, to bring up the ark of God the LORD who sits above the cherubim, the ark called by the Name. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:2 calls the place Baale Judah.

Arminian readers note that the ark’s title stresses the holy presence and authority of God himself, which raises the stakes of how it is handled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Chronicles identifies Baalah with Kiriath Jearim, where the ark had rested (1 Samuel 7:1–2), and that the description of the LORD enthroned above the cherubim prepares for the lesson about holiness that follows.

Both traditions read the verse as reverent preparation and see the ark as bearing the Name of the LORD.

verses.text: They carried God’s ark on a new cart, and brought it out of Abinadab’s house; and Uzza and Ahio drove the cart.
verses.arminianNotes:
They carry God’s ark on a new cart out of Abinadab’s house, with Uzza and Ahio driving. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:3 calls them the sons of Abinadab and spells the first name Uzzah.

Arminian readers note that the new cart resembles the Philistines’ method (1 Samuel 6:7) rather than the law’s instruction that the Kohathites bear the holy things, since “they carried it on their shoulders” (Numbers 7:9).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David himself later names this method as the root of the disaster (15:13), so that the fault lies first in the leaders’ plan rather than only in Uzza’s hand, and they read the cart as a well-intended but improper innovation.

Both traditions see the detail as preparing for the judgment that follows, and neither divides over it.

verses.text: David and all Israel played before God with all their might, even with songs, with harps, with stringed instruments, with tambourines, with cymbals, and with trumpets.
verses.arminianNotes:
David and all Israel play before God with all their might, with songs, harps, stringed instruments, tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:5 has a somewhat different list of instruments.

Arminian readers see sincere and wholehearted devotion here, and they affirm that earnest joy in worship is good and pleasing to God, which makes the sudden turn of the next verses all the more striking.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers agree that the joy is genuine, and they stress, as the notes on 2 Samuel 6:5 also observe, that enthusiasm in worship does not replace obedience to what God has said about approaching his presence.

Both traditions read the verse as real celebration that still needed to be joined to faithful obedience.

verses.text: When they came to Chidon’s threshing floor, Uzza put out his hand to hold the ark, for the oxen stumbled.
verses.arminianNotes:
At Chidon’s threshing floor Uzza puts out his hand to hold the ark, because the oxen stumble. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:6 names the place the threshing floor of Nacon, and the two names are simply recorded here.

Arminian readers see an act that seems instinctive and protective, and they acknowledge honestly the difficulty many readers feel at the judgment that follows.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise feel the weight of the moment, and they read the act in light of the law’s warning about the holy things: “they shall not touch the sanctuary, lest they die” (Numbers 4:15). The problem was approaching God’s holiness on human terms, beginning with the cart.

Both traditions read the verse soberly and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD’s anger burned against Uzza, and he struck him because he put his hand on the ark; and he died there before God.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s anger burns against Uzza, and he strikes him “because he put his hand on the ark”; Uzza dies there before God. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:7 says God struck him “for his error”.

Arminian readers read the judgment as a sober display of God’s holiness at a foundational moment for Israel’s worship, not as God acting arbitrarily, since God had made his requirements known beforehand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that God’s holiness is never safe to handle carelessly, even with good intentions, and that the whole procession shared the fault David later confesses in 15:13.

Both traditions acknowledge the difficulty of the verse, reject any picture of an arbitrary deity, keep the two accounts’ different wording, and read the verse as shared ground about holiness.

verses.text: David was displeased, because the LORD had broken out against Uzza. He called that place Perez Uzza, to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
David is displeased because the LORD has broken out against Uzza, and he names the place Perez Uzza, a name tied to that breaking out.

Arminian readers see honest human emotion in David’s reaction, recorded without condemnation, and they note that lament and perplexity before God can be part of a faithful life that keeps seeking him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the link with Baal Perazim in 14:11, where God breaks out against David’s enemies, so that the same divine power that delivers Israel also judges irreverence among them. Chronicles places that victory directly after this scene.

Both traditions read David’s displeasure as a stage in a process that leads him to learn and to obey.

verses.text: David was afraid of God that day, saying, “How can I bring God’s ark home to me?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David is afraid of God that day and asks, “How can I bring God’s ark home to me?” The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:9 has “How could the LORD’s ark come to me?”

Arminian readers see David’s fear turning him to question his approach, an honest response that leads him to seek the right way of worship rather than abandoning worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the fear as a fitting awareness of God’s holiness, and they note that the question is answered in 15:2 and 15:13, when David returns to the ordinance God gave through Moses.

Both traditions read the question as a turning point in the story and as shared ground about reverence before God.

verses.text: So David didn’t move the ark with him into David’s city, but carried it aside into Obed-Edom the Gittite’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
David does not move the ark into David’s city but takes it aside into the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite. The first attempt ends short of its goal.

Arminian readers see David pausing out of caution instead of pressing ahead, and they note that God’s presence is placed in an unexpected household that receives it and is blessed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Gittite usually means someone from Gath, and that some interpreters link this Obed-Edom with the Levite Obed-Edom of 15:18–24 and 16:38, though this is debated, as the notes on 2 Samuel 6:10 also observe.

Both traditions avoid deciding more than the text allows and read the verse as a pause, not an end.

verses.text: God’s ark remained with the family of Obed-Edom in his house three months; and the LORD blessed Obed-Edom’s house and all that he had.
verses.arminianNotes:
God’s ark remains with Obed-Edom’s family in his house three months, and the LORD blesses his house and all that he has.

Arminian readers see that God’s presence brings blessing to those who receive and honor it, a striking contrast with the judgment on Uzza, and an encouragement to approach God rightly rather than to fear him from a distance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the blessing as showing that God’s holiness is not hostile to his people when he is honored, and they note that Chronicles later lists Obed-Edom’s many sons with the remark that God blessed him (26:4–5), though whether that is the same man is debated.

Both traditions read the ark as bearing both blessing and danger.
